## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

BODY
The material contains four separable features, and it is worth keeping them separate because they call for different moves: recurring arguments over chores; agreements whose meaning gets contested later; work schedules that keep changing; and one friend now avoiding the conversations.

The most tractable is the contested-meaning problem. If you agree on who but not on what, when, or to what standard, later dispute is the expected outcome, not a mystery. 'You said you'd do the kitchen' can have meant wipe the counters tonight or deep-clean by Sunday, and both parties can honestly remember their version. A less charitable reading — someone reinterpreting to escape a load — is also possible, and the same remedy covers both cases without accusing anyone: capture the agreement in writing at the moment it is made. Task, concrete standard, deadline, somewhere all three can see. The asker can start this unilaterally: after any chore conversation, post a short confirmation — just so we're aligned, I've got X by Friday night, you've got Y by Sunday — that the others can correct on the spot. Once disputes are about a shared text rather than about memories, they get shorter even if nobody's motives improve.

Shifting schedules make fixed assignments brittle: a static rota either goes stale or lands unfairly. What fits that instability is short-horizon planning — a brief weekly look at who is actually around — plus an explicit swap rule: if your schedule changes, say so and propose a swap; do not let a task silently lapse. Silence after a schedule change is plausibly where a chunk of the later 'what did we agree' trouble originates.

The avoidance is the part where guessing is most tempting and most dangerous. One conjecture worth testing: if chore conversations only get convened when something has gone wrong, then 'let's talk about the chores' has become a synonym for complaint, and the friend may be avoiding being complained at — not the chores, not the asker. The word 'started' suggests this is a change rather than a fixed trait, which points toward something in the situation having shifted, possibly the character of the conversations themselves. If the conjecture holds, making the conversation routine, short, and mostly forward-looking (planning and swaps rather than audits) changes what it signals and may lower its cost. But that is a conjecture; the material does not say why the friend avoids the talks, and the difference matters — feeling ganged up on, feeling outvoted two-to-one, disengagement from the flat, and something entirely outside the chores each call for different responses. The move that fits the uncertainty is to ask, one-on-one and without accusation, what makes those conversations hard — and to do it before designing any system for that person rather than with them.

A caution against over-engineering: among friends, a visible enforcement apparatus can itself become the grievance, and the friendship is a bigger asset than any cleaning rota. Whatever system gets built should be minimal, jointly designed by all three so that it is ours rather than mine, and cheap to drop if it costs more goodwill than it saves.

One more conjecture worth testing quietly: chore arguments often run on a perception asymmetry — everyone sees their own contributions and few of anyone else's. If any of the arguing is about who does more, a shared visible record partially corrects each person's evidence. If the arguments are purely about task meaning, the record helps anyway.

And a fallback worth holding open rather than treating as defeat: if a fair, minimal, jointly adopted system is tried in good faith and the friction persists, the remaining options are structural — split a cleaner three ways, since money splits are more legible than labor splits; shrink the shared surface so there is less to argue about; or renegotiate whether the living arrangement is working. Those are legitimate endpoints, not failures.

In short: write agreements down as they are made; plan weekly against real schedules with a swap rule; ask the avoidant friend what is hard before assuming; keep the system light and jointly owned; and keep structural exits in view.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
